name: Open society
summary: The open society is Karl Popper's ideal of a free society in which rulers can be removed peacefully, institutions are open to criticism and reform step by step, and individuals, not the state, nation or class, are the ultimate concern. It opposes totalitarianism, historicism, nationalism and the claim that anyone is born to rule, and allows the state to protect the weak from economic power.

sources.usedFor: Peer-reviewed scholarship on the concept: Bergson's origin, Popper's conception, and how the term has come to carry several senses (Introduction, chapter on the communitarian conception).

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 10 'The Open Society and Its Enemies': the closed society's institutions, including its castes, are 'sacrosanct - taboo', whereas competition for status among its members is 'one of the most important characteristics of the open society'. Popper describes this as the open society's character rather than proposing a law, so +1.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: Soros, Open Society: Reforming Global Capitalism (2000), ch. 5 'Open Society as an Ideal': the need for 'international law and international institutions' to settle common interests. Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), Notes to ch. 9, note 7: Popper compares international institutions (legislative, administrative, judicial) with those within the state, and wants a police force ready to act against international crime. Binding arbitration is not named, so +1.

ban-cartels.rationale: Popper cites anti-trust legislation, with taxation and death duties, as means to counteract centralisation of economic power, while doubting how effective it is.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: In the note on the paradox of tolerance Popper claims the right not to tolerate the intolerant, holds that a movement preaching intolerance places itself outside the law, and says attacks on the democratic constitution may be resisted by all loyal citizens.

basic-income.rationale: Scholars report Popper supported a minimum income for all citizens as a means of abolishing poverty, though he also wrote of guaranteeing a livelihood to those willing to work.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Popper argues that Marx's prophecy of collapse fails because legislation, taxation and social insurance have transformed the unrestrained capitalism Marx described.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Popper writes that he is against imposing one's likes and dislikes upon others and against censorship in matters of art, and he treats Plato's censorship as a mark of totalitarianism.

central-planning.rationale: Popper opposes holistic planning of whole societies as inevitably disastrous because consequences cannot be foreseen, and warns that too much planning destroys freedom and thereby planning itself.

change-traditions-that-no-longer-suit.rationale: Popper asks for a critical attitude toward tradition, to be freed of its taboo status by asking whether to accept or reject it, while also stressing tradition's value for order.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Popper denies laws of historical development, holds political power to be fundamental and able to control economic power, and rejects Marx's ranking of class relations over politics.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 12 'Hegel and the New Tribalism': describes nationalism as appealing 'to our tribal instincts, to passion and to prejudice' and as part of the revolt against the open society; it offers no support for claims on land abroad.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 12 'Hegel and the New Tribalism' (and ch. 1): rejects Hegel's and the nationalists' view that struggle between nations and races drives history; the progress Popper values comes from criticism and peaceful reform.

corporate-influence.rationale: Popper holds that economic power must not be allowed to dominate political power and must be brought under control by it, which bears on lobbying though he does not discuss lobbying itself.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Popper's paradox of democracy shows that a majority may choose a tyrant, so he holds the majority principle needs institutional safeguards and the democratic constitution defended.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Popper proposes that all citizens be insured by law against disability, unemployment and old age, and counts protection from starvation as a condition of freedom, which contradicts cutting such programmes.

decide-locally.rationale: Soros, Open Society: Reforming Global Capitalism (2000), ch. 5 'Open Society as an Ideal' (end of the section before 'The Principles of Open Society'): 'the principle of subsidiarity: ... decisions should be made at the lowest possible level.'

democracy-best.rationale: Popper holds that democracy is the only framework that lets a people reform its institutions without violence, and says it cannot supply wisdom in its citizens; he defends it without assuming voters are wise (Open Society I ch. 7).

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Popper defines democracy by the ability to dismiss a government without bloodshed through elections, not by the policies it adopts, and demands only that rulers be controlled by and accountable to the public.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Popper criticises a revolution that seeks complete political power for one class with a resolve not to shrink from violence, and demands a government that can be dismissed without bloodshed.

direct-action.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 7 'The Principle of Leadership' and ch. 19: democratic institutions, especially general elections, are the means of public control and reform without violence; direct action is not offered as a replacement.

direct-votes.rationale: Scholarship reports that Popper replaced rule by the people and popular initiative with judgement by the people of policies, which tells against citizens legislating directly.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Popper attacks the Platonic and Nazi racial theory of breeding and purity, and bases politics on equal treatment of individuals regardless of birth.

divinely-chosen-superior-people.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 1 'Historicism and the Myth of Destiny' (the chosen-people doctrine) and ch. 4 (the myth of racial superiority): attacked as a historicist and racialist myth of the closed society.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Popper's individualism is the opposite of the collectivist principle that the individual exists to maintain the community, which he calls the tribal totalitarian theory of morality.

elective-rulers.rationale: Popper's test of democracy is that a government can be dismissed without bloodshed, which a hereditary ruler cannot be, though he does not discuss monarchy directly.

elite-replacement.rationale: Popper rejects the conspiracy theory of society that explains social events by the designs of a powerful group, as unscientific and dangerous.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Popper argues that an international organisation with legislative, judicial and administrative bodies and an armed police force could uphold peace as institutions do within a state.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Soros, Open Society: Reforming Global Capitalism (2000), ch. 5 'Open Society as an Ideal' (The Principles of Open Society): a condition of open society is 'constitutional protection for minority rights'; ch. 12 'The Open Society Alliance' names a democratic constitution and an independent judiciary as preconditions. Entrenchment against ordinary majorities is not stated in so many words, so +1.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Popper's equalitarian principle demands that citizens be treated impartially, with birth, family connection or wealth never influencing the law, and he grounds this in humanitarian individualism.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Popper says freedom is more important than equality and that the attempt to realise equality endangers freedom, while his equalitarian principle demands only equal treatment before the law.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Popper calls the principle that a state should coincide with one nation an irrational, romantic and utopian dream of naturalism and tribal collectivism.

experts-over-public.rationale: Popper rejects rule by a wise elite and leaves the public to judge policy, yet his piecemeal reform is run by technical experts, and scholars call his open society technocratic.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Popper holds that nobody should be at the mercy of others and that all should be protected by the state, applying this to economic as well as physical power.

gradual-change.rationale: Popper advocates altering one social institution at a time and reforming institutions little by little, as the only method of improvement that has succeeded anywhere.

harm-principle.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 17 'The Legal and the Social System' (paradox of freedom) and ch. 6 'Totalitarian Justice': the state's task is to protect citizens' freedom, limiting it only to the extent needed so that freedom is not destroyed by the strong. Not given as a general harm principle, so +1.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Popper calls mistaken the idea that citizens' quality can be raised by institutional eugenic control, and criticises Plato's breeding proposals as part of the closed society.

human-decline-since-golden-age.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 3 and ch. 10: Plato's law of decay from a perfect origin is criticised as part of the historicist and tribalist reaction; ch. 10 treats longing for a lost harmonious past as a romantic escape from the strain of civilization.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 12 'Hegel and the New Tribalism' and ch. 4: nationalism is an appeal to tribal instincts and part of the revolt against the open society; ch. 4 rejects racialist myths. Popper does not discuss kin-state union as such, so -1.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 20 'Capitalism and Its Fate': examines the hypothesis that workers' gains came from colonial exploitation and rejects it as an explanation of the rise in workers' conditions.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 20 'Capitalism and Its Fate', section II (the theory of value): argues that once wages are admitted not to correspond to values, the labour theory of value is 'utterly destroyed', and judges Marx's rescue by surplus value unnecessary for his main argument.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Popper argues that no theory that a nation is united by common language, origin or history is acceptable or usable in practice.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 5 'Nature and Convention': laws and norms are man-made conventions to be criticised and changed, not derived from authority or revelation.

leader-cult.rationale: Popper calls the worship of power and the ethics of hero-worship among the worst of servitudes and rejects the leader principle.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 17 'The Legal and the Social System': Popper says the defenders of unrestrained capitalism are right to stress 'the tremendous benefit to be derived from the mechanism of free markets', but adds that unrestrained markets need a legal framework and intervention (paradox of freedom). Soros, Open Society: Reforming Global Capitalism (2000), ch. 5 (The Principles of Open Society): freedom of choice 'allows the market mechanism to operate', and the state has not proved the best agency for meeting economic needs. Positive but qualified, so +1.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Popper takes the directly opposite view to Marx that economic evolution determines politics: he treats political power as fundamental and humanitarian faith with critical reason as able to change the world.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Popper rejects the conspiracy theory of society, which explains social ills by the plots of groups, as a mistaken doctrine that leads its holders to act on it.

morality-needs-religion.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 5 'Nature and Convention': moral norms are man-made and decided by us, and a humanitarian ethics is held independently of religious authority. Popper also respects Christian ethics, so only -1.

nation-first.rationale: Popper holds that individuals, not states or nations, are the ultimate concern even of international organisations, and calls the national state principle a tribal instinct, which tells against putting one's nation first.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), Notes to ch. 9, note 7, and ch. 12 'Hegel and the New Tribalism': Popper favours international institutions with a force ready to act against international crime, and describes nationalism as an appeal to tribal instincts. Soros, Open Society: Reforming Global Capitalism (2000), ch. 5: national sovereignty 'has to be subordinated to the international common good'.

national-rebirth.rationale: Popper opposes romantic nationalist calls for a return to the tribe as reaction against the open society.

national-self-determination.rationale: Popper rejects the principle of the national state, that every nation should have its own state, as never clearly conceived and a myth, though he notes nationalism was once a liberal creed.

natural-rulers.rationale: Popper writes that personal superiority, racial, intellectual, moral or educational, can never establish a claim to political prerogatives, even if it could be ascertained.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Popper explicitly gives up the principle of non-intervention in the economy and calls his view protectionism, the state protecting the economically weak from the strong, which goes beyond a minimal state.

one-party-rule.rationale: Popper treats a single party tolerating no other, ruling in the name of a correct doctrine, as the mark of the totalitarian closed society that he opposes.

opposition-only-legal-channels.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 19 'Social Revolution': under a tyranny that makes reform without violence impossible, violent revolution 'may be justified', so Popper does not confine opposition to legal channels there.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Scholarship reports that Popper held public policy is not to be made through the inclusive public deliberation of participatory democracy; the public's role is to judge government.

party-controls-media.rationale: Popper's open society rests on freedom of thought and criticism, and he condemns the rigid censorship of the closed society, which rules out government or party control of the media.

patriotic-education.rationale: Popper warns that too much state control of education leads to indoctrination, and treats nationalism as a tribal, romantic creed, which tells against teaching national pride.

person-over-state.rationale: Popper's humanitarian individualism holds that the state and institutions exist to serve individuals and never the reverse, and that the collective has no needs prior to those of living persons.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 7 'The Principle of Leadership': political authority is to be controlled through institutions that let the ruled dismiss rulers, not rest on personal allegiance; the question 'Who shall rule?' is rejected.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 19 'Social Revolution': violence is justified only against tyranny and in defence of democracy once attained; otherwise reform should be non-violent (see also ch. 7, democracy as the framework for reform without violence).

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Soros, Open Society: Reforming Global Capitalism (2000), ch. 5 'Open Society as an Ideal': 'national sovereignty has to be subordinated to the international common good', through international law and institutions, though 'it does not lead us to a global state'. A general statement, not about the European Union specifically, so +1.

positive-liberty.rationale: Popper holds that economic dependence can strip people of freedom as surely as violence and that the state must protect against economic fear, though he does not frame freedom in terms of positive liberty.

power-shapes-accepted-knowledge.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 23 'The Sociology of Knowledge': rejects the claim that knowledge is determined by social position or interest; objectivity rests on the public, critical institutions of science. Popper allows that interests influence thought, so -1.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Popper holds that suffering makes a direct moral appeal for help and treats poverty and unemployment as the first targets of public policy.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: Soros, Open Society: Reforming Global Capitalism (2000), Introduction and ch. 12 'The Open Society Alliance': proposes an alliance of democratic states whose objectives include 'to strengthen democracy within individual countries' and to promote the values and principles of open society, while leaving 'each society the greatest possible latitude'. Soros's own proposal rather than a defining principle, so +1.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 17 'The Legal and the Social System': prefers 'institutional' intervention through a legal framework that citizens can know and understand, with predictable working, over discretionary 'personal' intervention by rulers or civil servants.

proportional-representation.rationale: Scholarship reports that Popper opposed proportional representation because coalition governments blur responsibility and make elections less meaningful than a two-party system.

public-ownership.rationale: Popper notes that state ownership of industry and transport brought no clearly beneficial results and calls its benefit doubtful, though he favours state intervention in general.

racial-franchise.rationale: Popper holds that no racial superiority could create special political rights, and calls racialism a myth of the closed society, so restricting the franchise to one race contradicts his equalitarian principle.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Popper treats racialism as the closed society's myth and demands equal treatment before the law irrespective of birth, which excludes laws classifying and separating people by race.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Popper defends faith in reason and humanitarianism as the basis of the open society but treats rationalism as resting on a decision that reason alone cannot compel, so he neither affirms nor denies reason as the only guide.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Popper wants the state to protect the economically weak from the economically strong, and notes anti-trust law and taxation as tools, though he warns that intervention enlarges state power.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Popper says a government that misuses its powers or tolerates tyranny outlaws itself, and that citizens have a right and a duty to resist it, even by violence.

restore-past-order.rationale: Popper presents the return to the tribe's closed order as the reaction he opposes, in favour of reform of institutions by reason.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Popper holds that incitement to intolerance and persecution should be treated as criminal like incitement to murder, though he says nothing on speech that merely offends.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Popper urges testing each reform by its results and correcting it, the piecemeal method against blueprints that must be followed whatever the outcome.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 10 'The Open Society and Its Enemies' (end of the section on Plato): 'We can never return to the alleged innocence and beauty of the closed society'; once we rely on reason and feel personal responsibility we cannot return to tribal submission. Hunter-gatherer life is not named, so -1.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 19 'Social Revolution': 'I am not in all cases and under all circumstances against a violent revolution' but it is justified only under a tyranny that makes reform without violence impossible, with democracy as its sole aim. Conditional acceptance as an exception, so -1.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Soros, Open Society: Reforming Global Capitalism (2000), ch. 5 'Open Society as an Ideal' (human rights and social justice passage): 'it behooves the rich to come to the aid of the poor; therefore social justice is a matter of international concern', with a 'more level playing field' as an objective of international institutions.

rule-by-example.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 7 'The Principle of Leadership': replaces the question 'who shall rule?' with how rulers can be controlled by institutions (checks and balances); ch. 17 prefers legal framework to rulers' discretion.

sacred-nation.rationale: Popper treats the worship of the nation or state as a collectivist, tribal doctrine that sets the group above the persons it consists of.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Popper's open society treats institutions as man-made and rulers as answerable, and sets this against the taboo-bound tribal order with sacred rulers.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 6 'Totalitarian Justice': distinguishes individualism from egoism and defends individualism together with altruism; egoism is not offered as a moral basis.

separated-powers.rationale: Popper calls for the institutional control of rulers by balancing their power against other powers, the checks-and-balances idea, as the practical safeguard against tyranny.

single-common-good.rationale: Popper rejects utopian blueprints for a single ideal good, and holds that ultimate human ends such as freedom and equality conflict, so politics should address concrete evils instead.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 12 'Hegel and the New Tribalism': describes nationalism as a tribalist revolt against the open society and notes that European states have been 'inter-tribal' of mixed populations since Alexander; no support for merging regions into ethnic units.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 9 'Aestheticism, Perfectionism, Utopianism': piecemeal engineering reconstructs institutions bit by bit in the light of experience, against holistic reconstruction. The statement's wording is 'respect established institutions'; Popper's reform works through and on existing institutions but he also urges a critical attitude to tradition, so +1 not +2.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 9 'Aestheticism, Perfectionism, Utopianism' and ch. 19: rejects wholesale reconstruction of society; revolution is allowed only to establish democracy under a tyranny.

social-market-economy.rationale: Soros, Open Society: Reforming Global Capitalism (2000), ch. 5 'Open Society as an Ideal' (section 'The Principles of Open Society'): the list of conditions of an open society includes 'a market economy that respects property rights and provides opportunities and a safety net for the disadvantaged'. Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), vol. 2 ch. 17 'The Legal and the Social System' (sections on economic intervention) and ch. 18 'The Coming of Socialism' likewise endorse democratic interventionism with social insurance.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Popper's paradox of sovereignty shows that any ruler above control can become a tyrant, and he demands that rulers be controlled by and accountable to the public.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Popper rejects Marx's view that politics is the least important power, arguing that democratic political power can control economic power and has done so in the modern democracies.

state-harmful.rationale: Popper holds that freedom is impossible unless the state guarantees it, and calls state power a necessary though dangerous evil.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: Popper warns that state pursuit of an ideal of happiness leads to imposing a scale of higher values on others in order to save their souls, and prefers the state to relieve concrete suffering.

strong-leader.rationale: Popper's remedy for tyranny is institutional control of rulers, and he condemns the leader principle, so a leader overriding institutional checks runs against his position.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Popper demands a government controlled by and accountable to the public and protected criticism of policy, so suppressing opposition and independent organisations contradicts his position.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Popper notes that heavy death duties counteract centralisation of wealth but calls it doubtful whether more would be desirable, so his view leans toward but does not clearly demand heavy taxation.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 18 'The Coming of Socialism': counting Marx's programme, Popper lists 'a heavy progressive or graduated income tax' as 'carried out' in the democracies, among the steps toward social security, while remarking that more death duties are 'doubtful'. He treats it as an achieved democratic measure, not as something he demands much more of, so +1.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Popper condemns the totalitarian state-worship that holds a state may attack others whenever it is strong, and the imperialist tendencies of modern totalitarianism.

total-state.rationale: Popper's critique of totalitarianism rejects a state that directs every area of life as the central political evil of the closed society.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Popper opposes both racialist fascism and Marxist historicism as forms of the totalitarian revolt against the open society, though he does not call them equivalent in every respect.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 12 'Hegel and the New Tribalism': traces nationalism to a revival (in mixed Germany/Prussia) of the tribal Platonic-Aristotelian nationalism, an appeal to tribal instincts, passion and prejudice; the nations of Europe are of 'infinitely mixed origin', not units of unbroken ancestry.

unions-good.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 20 'Capitalism and Its Fate': discusses how trade unions and legislation raised workers' conditions and refuted Marx's prediction of increasing misery; the account is favourable to what unions achieved. Not a central theme, so +1.

universal-morality.rationale: Soros, Open Society: Reforming Global Capitalism (2000), ch. 5 'Open Society as an Ideal', 'The Principles of Open Society': distinguishes 'timelessly, universally valid principles' (freedoms, human rights, rule of law, social responsibility and justice) from a time-bound description, while allowing that different epochs and societies may define them differently. Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 22 'The Moral Theory of Historicism', rejects moral relativism and defends a universal humanitarian ethics.

wages-fall-to-bare-minimum.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 20 'Capitalism and Its Fate': Marx's law of increasing misery is refuted by experience; unions, legislation and social insurance raised workers' standards.

war-builds-character.rationale: Popper attacks the Heraclitean and Hegelian glorification of war and strife as part of the revolt against the open society.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Popper holds that economic power can be as dangerous as physical violence, that the economically strong can bully the weak out of their freedom, and that economic power must not dominate political power.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1962 ed.), ch. 17 'The Legal and the Social System': calls 'economic democracy' 'a vague and utterly superficial phrase' that obscures that 'merely formal freedom' is the only guarantee of a democratic economic policy.

missingStatements.text: Public policy should aim at reducing suffering, not at achieving an ideal of happiness.
missingStatements.rationale: Popper's negative utilitarianism makes relieving concrete suffering the task of policy and rejects state pursuit of ideal happiness.

quotes.text: a systematic fight against suffering and injustice and war is more likely to be supported by the approval and agreement of a great number of people than the fight for the establishment of some ideal
human suffering makes a direct moral appeal, namely, the appeal for help, while there is no similar call to increase the happiness of a man who is doing well anyway
quotes.where: popper.txt, vol. II ch. 24 note, lines 23815-23817

missingStatements.text: The course of history is not governed by laws.
missingStatements.rationale: Popper rejects historicism: no law of progress or historical necessity determines the future.

quotes.text: The future depends on ourselves, and we do not depend on any historical necessity.
There is no law of progress, and everything will depend on ourselves.

missingStatements.declined: A philosophical claim; covered by material-conditions-drive-history.

scope: Popper's open society, the subject of The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945): a society that subjects its traditions and institutions to criticism, confronts individuals with personal decisions and responsibility, lets citizens remove rulers and reform policies without violence, step by step, and treats the state as serving individuals; its enemies are historicism, holism and collectivism (Plato, Hegel, Marx), totalitarianism and claims to ultimate truth (IEP, SEP, Encyclopedia of Science, Technology, and Ethics). The term and the open/closed distinction come from Henri Bergson's The Two Sources of Morality and Religion; the sources say Bergson's openness was spiritual and Popper's secular and experimental, so Bergson's own doctrine is not part of this profile beyond the shared distinction (Encyclopedia of Science, Technology, and Ethics). Soros's Open Society: Reforming Global Capitalism (2000) is read as a later thinker's account that adopts Popper's concept (open society as an imperfect society open to improvement, a global open society, a critique of market fundamentalism), and counts only where he states what an open society is or requires. Left out: J. McKenzie Alexander's four 'conceptions' (cosmopolitan, transparent, Enlightenment, communitarian) and Fischer's comparison of New Zealand and the United States, which are their own constructions of the term; Bergson's mysticism; the grant-making of the Open Society Foundations, an organisation; open government and open source; and critics of Popper (Cornforth), who do not answer.

keyFigures.role: Philosopher who coined the terms open and closed society in The Two Sources of Morality and Religion

evidence.quote: The term open society was first introduced by Henri Bergson in 1932 when he published his Two Sources of Religion and Morality.
In his seminal work Two Sources of Morality and Religion - where the concept of the Open Society first appeared - Henri Bergson characterised the closed society

keyWorks.title: The Open Society and Its Enemies

evidence.quote: Indeed, his most important political texts— The Poverty of Historicism (1944) and The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945)—offer a kind of unified vision of science and politics.
The Open Society and Its Enemies

Although Henri Bergson (1859–1941) first employed the term open society in The Two Sources of Morality and Religion (1935) and Eric Voegelin (1901–1985) made Bergson's interpretation a key concept in his philosophy of history, it was The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945) by Karl R. Popper (1902–1994) that gave the phrase wide currency.

Although Henri Bergson (1859–1941) first employed the term open society in The Two Sources of Morality and Religion (1935) and Eric Voegelin (1901–1985) made Bergson's interpretation a key concept in his philosophy of history, it was The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945) by Karl R. Popper (1902–1994) that gave the phrase wide currency.
The terms ‘open society’ and ‘closed society’ were first used, to my knowledge, by Henri Bergson, in Two Sources of Morality and Religion (Engl. ed., 1935).
